newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Surging oil output to ease stock deficit, cap prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Surging oil output to ease stock deficit, cap prices.

text.p: World oil demand will jump sharply this winter but extra supplies from new non-OPEC fields, delayed from earlier this year, should ease severe stock shortages and may keep a cap on oil prices, analysts say.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday global oil demand will rise to 73.8 million barrels per day (bpd) in the fourth quarter 1996, up 1.9 million year on year.

But supply should easily keep pace with demand, the IEA said, at an estimated 73.7 million bpd which includes a 1.8 million increase in supplies outside the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"My feeling about the market is that we will soon be balanced to surplus oil supplies for the first time in many, many months," said Geoff Pyne, energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.
In mid-October, oil prices hit their highest levels since the Gulf War of 1991 amid Middle East tensions, buoyant demand and fears that low heating oil stocks will fall short in the winter.
But since then, prices have slid nearly $3 a barrel as U.S. and European refineries run flat-out to replenish low inventories of distillates used to heat homes.
Unless the winter is exceptionally cold, analysts say, inventories should soon near more normal levels.

"From the second quarter 1997, we see a constant build on stocks. I think the market will take note early on so any price spike will be sold into," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, an oil consultant at Petroleum Finance Corp (PFC).

Industry stocks held in members nations of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) at end-September stood a sharp 91 million barrels under 1995 levels and distillates comprised more than half the deficit, the IEA said.

But the stock shortfall was expected to "decrease appreciably" in the fourth quarter, the agency said, because of the "historically" high stock draw in fourth quarter 1995 and since non-OPEC output is expected to surge.
"There is the potential for an appreciable reduction in the year-on-year shortfall by the end of the year," the IEA said.
Resilient oil markets, surprising pundits into hurried upward price forecast revisions of at least $3 a barrel, have enticed producers to pump up volumes.
The IEA said non-OPEC output leapt by 830,000 bpd in October to 44.2 million and should average 45 million over the fourth quarter, a massive 2.2 million increase from fourth quarter 1995.
The gains are even more significant because lower-than-expected non-OPEC output increase helped pave the way for this year's oil price rally.
But the tide now has turned, the IEA said, and the kinks that had hampered the start-up of several new oil developments have been hammered out.
"There is some evidence that the periods of downward revisions in non-OPEC supply estimates may be coming to an end," the IEA said.
Meanwhile, OPEC output in October topped 26 million bpd for the first time since 1980 when OPEC had 13 members, two more than now, the IEA said.

OPEC output is running about a million bpd over its self-imposed 25.03 million bpd ceiling and does not even include the full 1.2 million bpd assigned to Iraq since a much-delayed UN oil-for-food sale has yet to be implemented.
"We see gradual increases in OPEC production even without Iraq so when it (Iraq) does come in, we have to see some downward price pressure," PFC's Abduljabbar said.
